summary:
Kostroma Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full. The dedicated assessment of this region identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately, and the oblast is therefore assessed at the national score.

For a trans traveller the national position means that legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and same-sex marriage is banned. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. The expanded law criminalises public expression that justifies gender transition. Foreigners who violate these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation.

Since the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the international LGBT movement as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and three criminal, as of 30 June 2025.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment. A further 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention risk, the war and arbitrary law enforcement, and its advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Enforcement has escalated in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget over two years. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. In July 2024 the BBC reported on a transgender woman lured by relatives in 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. The same note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave is national in scope, with no Kostroma-specific incident recorded in the sources. The documented raids and arrests concentrate in the largest cities: Moscow venues were searched within two days of the extremist designation, and St Petersburg has been a recurring site of extremism charges. These are illustrations of a countrywide pattern rather than a separate regional risk profile.

Reported outcomes for those caught in the designation are severe and include death in custody. A man held on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility in December 2024.

Conditions in some constituent territories are worse than the national baseline. The UK Home Office note names the autonomous republic of Chechnya alongside the country as a whole when affirming refugee-convention protection, which indicates that the particular-social-group finding is not limited to the federal centres.

Volume of enforcement is rising independently of severity: propaganda-law cases have multiplied eighteenfold over a decade, and the administrative route under article 20.3 produced 98 convictions in an eighteen-month window, meaning low-threshold charges carry most of the caseload.
localsOnly:
Residents face a closed set of legal options. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned in 2023, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and same-sex marriage is not available, so there is no lawful route to align documents with presentation.

Participation in the designated international LGBT movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Displaying alleged symbols is prosecuted administratively under article 20.3, which accounted for 81 convictions in 98 cases between January 2024 and June 2025.

Repeat propaganda offences are prosecuted under the criminal code with up to four years' imprisonment, and article 282.2 charges have been brought against publishing-house staff who face up to 12 years. At least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution and that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims and treats LGBT+ people as a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Forced conversion practice is documented: a transgender woman was held for nine months at a centre near Novosibirsk from summer 2021, forced to take testosterone and perform manual labour, and only left after police responded to a phone she had found.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kostroma Oblast-specific enforcement data, court record or incident report appears in the source inventory. The regional assessment rests on the absence of identified deviation from the national position, which is a scoring finding rather than evidence of local practice, and local enforcement intensity remains unverified.

The sources do not establish whether any healthcare facility, support organisation or safe venue operates within the oblast following the 2023 care ban; availability of services on the ground is not sourced.

The eighteenfold rise in propaganda-law cases and the 60 million rubles in fines are national aggregates with no regional breakdown, so the oblast's share of that caseload is unresolved.

The conversion-therapy case documented by the BBC occurred near Novosibirsk and the pretrial death reported by the Associated Press is not located in the oblast; neither is attributed to Kostroma Oblast.

Whether the 101 extremism convictions include any proceeding initiated in this oblast is not stated in the inventory.
